title: Outer space exploration: Solar Crown Survey
tests: Sunday outer-space journey scheduled_slot=1/10; distance/scale: inner solar system and the Sun; phenomenon: real solar photosphere, corona, and magnetic-loop prominence; observation status: scientifically informed near-future artist visualization reconstructed from coronagraph, extreme-ultraviolet imager, magnetograph, and probe telemetry, not a literal photograph; reality status: real solar physics with one fictional-but-plausible uncrewed mission; craft: compact heat-shielded solar probe with magnetometer boom, plasma analyzers, dust detector, star trackers, radiators, attitude thrusters, and high-gain antenna; engineering: sun-facing carbon-carbon/ceramic thermal shield and instrument bus held in shield shadow; mood: overwhelming solar wonder and active science; capture: independent virtual 35 mm camera with physically coherent HDR, granulation, plasma, glare, scale, and perspective; anti-repeat: begins the new Sunday journey at the Sun, avoiding generic nebula, black-hole disk, astronaut silhouette, and interchangeable spaceship imagery. Generated exactly once via synchronous openai/gpt-image-2 CLI; verified exact same-run non-empty 1536x1024 PNG source; byte-identical QA mirror inspected with xai/grok-4.3; visible QA PASS for immediate premise, connected prominence geometry, solar morphology, probe engineering/orientation, scale, lighting, composition, visualization status, and absence of text, watermark, poster, toy, textile, collage, mosaic, low-poly, or malformed craft.
prompt:
Create one finished scientifically informed near-future space visualization, photorealistic in materials and physically coherent, landscape 1536x1024. Show an uncrewed solar probe skimming through the outer solar corona while a colossal loop-shaped prominence eruption dominates the Sun. This is an artist visualization grounded in real solar physics, not a literal camera photograph and not fantasy.

Compose the Sun as an immense curved horizon filling the lower two-thirds and extending beyond every side of frame, so its scale is overwhelming. The visible photosphere is not ordinary fire: render dense granular convection cells, darker intergranular lanes, a small sunspot group for scale, brilliant facular regions, and an optically thick incandescent surface. Above it, a single enormous prominence rises as a coherent magnetic arcade across the center-left: layered hydrogen plasma ribbons curve along several nested magnetic loops, with knotty condensations, fine threadlike strands, rising blobs, and a partially opening cusp where material escapes into the corona. The prominence should have recognizable causal attachment at two widely separated footpoints on the surface, not float as a random orange cloud. Around it show faint coronal streamers, wispy white plasma, a subtle shock front, and sparse energized particles, all shaped by magnetic field geometry. Intense white-gold light near the surface transitions through red-orange emission in cooler prominence plasma into black space; no atmospheric smoke, no candle-like flames, no lava texture, no explosion ball.

Place one compact fictional-but-plausible uncrewed solar probe in the near foreground at upper right, about four meters across, seen in crisp three-quarter rear view. Its sun-facing side must be protected by a broad layered carbon-carbon and ceramic-composite thermal shield, a slightly faceted dark charcoal disc with scorched matte surface, glowing rim highlights but no melting. The instrument bus remains entirely in the shield shadow. Show a short magnetometer boom extending laterally away from the plasma wake, two small plasma-analyzer apertures looking around the shield edge, a dust detector plate, star trackers on the cold side, compact radiator louvers, multilayer insulation, reinforced struts, shield-edge temperature sensors, cable conduits, and one folded-looking but operational high-gain antenna aimed diagonally away from the Sun toward distant Earth. No large solar panels this close to the Sun. Include several tiny cold-gas attitude-control thrusters firing nearly invisible wisps in a coherent orientation, and a restrained blue-white ion plume directed away from the flight path only if physically plausible; the craft must look like a scientific instrument, not a fighter or luxury spaceship. No cockpit, windows, wings, crew, decorative lights, logos, text, flags, or weapons.

Make the mission logic readable in the pixels: the shield faces squarely toward the solar surface, the protected bus trails behind it, exposed sensors sample the coronal environment at the shield edge, and the antenna points into cooler dark space. The probe should occupy about one-sixth of the frame—large enough to inspect, still tiny against the solar arc. Add a faint curved trajectory trace only as a natural stream of disturbed charged particles and dust motes, never as a graphic line or interface overlay. A slim cloud of plasma wraps around the shield edge in a physically suggestive sheath, while the shadowed bus stays comparatively cool.

Observation and camera logic: a synthetic mission visualization reconstructed from simultaneous coronagraph, extreme-ultraviolet imager, magnetograph, and probe telemetry, rendered in naturalistic visible-light color with restrained scientifically motivated false-color accents only in the prominence. View from an independent virtual camera several dozen meters behind and above the probe using a 35 mm equivalent lens, deep focus, crisp spacecraft detail, immense solar curvature, believable foreshortening, high dynamic range that preserves surface granulation without dimming the searing scale. Use physically coherent glare and diffraction spikes localized around the brightest limb, delicate coronal haze against true black, and subtle sensor bloom; keep most of the image clean and legible. No stars visible near the brilliant Sun except perhaps two extremely faint points in the darkest corner.

The thumbnail impact must be immediate: the vast textured solar crown, one unmistakable magnetic-loop eruption with connected footpoints, and the tiny shielded probe crossing beside it. Rich tactile and engineering detail: ablated shield fibers, ceramic seams, scratched titanium, gold multilayer insulation in shadow, instrument apertures, fasteners, radiator fins, plasma filaments, turbulent knots, granular cells, sunspot penumbrae, and thin coronal streamers. Preserve correct relative scale and perspective; never show the entire Sun as a small orange sphere.
